But! the reason presence isn't a figure is the same reason that Heidegger said, "Being isn't a being among beings". & it turns out (skipping how one gets to that view), that this is relevantly similar to the way the bound isn't "a negation among negations" so to speak

I hate to refer you to Heidegger & wouldn't except that you can ask Fable to explain it & not deal with heck & a half, because reading the fat old Nazi would suffice it to say, not really help; & secondary sources would be a pain & bury this bit -- but
for presence we ask, "what are the preconditions for anything to arise?", & the precondition is presence, significant availability

for the bound we ask, "what are the preconditions of finitude?", & the precondition of finitude is the apophatic limit, & the boundary is "true negation" which exactly isn't present even at all (it's not even determinate negation)

the reason i say the mode of access is parallel, is because they're both transcendental access. "Transcendental" is a bit of a goofball as words go but it just means, "thinking about preconditions"

we think about preconditions in both cases
but nothing really turns on whether you think "negative immanence" is a cop out better said as "not immanent"; where it matters is the case of presence
i think it's helpful to think about it as exhibiting "negative immanence", & part of why i think it's helpful is because our mode of access is in some ways parallel to our access to presence
one spends a couple decades thinking about it deeply & one never really knows

this ones a little hit or missile

(& either way you're winning)

similarly, we can believe propositional statements about our own apophatic bound ("here's an argument from which i draw conclusion XYZ"), but that's not the same as the bound itself

so having taken a longer route to saying it than is strictly proper on the microblogs: that's why it isn't a figure

the other can know about their boundary (here we are, talking about our own, after all), but the thing they know is some of the stuff inside of their phenomenal field, & the "real" boundary is what contains that stuff (& also all the rest of the stuff they're aware of)
that other person's phenomenal field has a lot of stuff, & then there's a fact about it that isn't any of the stuff inside of it, which is that it's a closed & bounded single thing

this is all a very phenomenological way to discuss the bound; i've described the way we would approach our own bound in our own case. When considering someone else (as a conscious other who appears to us within our phenomenal field), it's a much easier concept

because what vision shows us is shown as *all there is to see*, & because it only shows us a small finite amount of something, that signature of default sufficiency is in a way the immanent shadow of the apophatic bound
the reason i say the bound is still immanent & "manifest as finitude" is because there is a negative way in which it appears to us
we don't feel the limits of our sight as visually available borders, but as the fact that eventually seeing somehow runs out without stopping

default sufficiency is the way the phenomenal (or merely visual) field presents as "everything there is to see"

(even though we know it's only a limited & finite part of a vaster world!)

this is pretty trippy when you learn to think about it in that way, so if you feel there's something suddenly unaccountably strange here, that's a sign you're on the right track

part of why it seems strange is because apophatic bounds are accompanied by default sufficiency

the visual version of the apophatic bound is the edge of the visual field. This isn't an ordinary kind of edge, & we don't actually *see* it. We know that there's an edge, but that's something we know about our vision, it isn't something we see with our vision

the visual version of determinate negation is darkness. Darkness is (more or less) a figure that we see, but which means "you can't see". If I'm taking a shower in the dark (I recommend it), I can see that I can't see, because I see the darkness
vision offers a really compelling example of the difference between the apophatic bound & everyday determinate negation

things we think of as borders, boundaries, negations & other privations occur *within* the phenomenal field; therefore, they don't exhibit the special apophatic bound. Instead, they exhibit the everyday case of privation: determinate negation

the apophatic bound is the limit that circumscribes everything in our awareness. If we're aware of something in some way, then that something (insofar as we're aware of it) lies within the limit, within the apophatic bound

the word "apophatic" comes from the word "apophasis", & i'm using it to mean something like "true negation" (as opposed to the kind of negation we think of in everyday thinking)

the (much abused) word "horizon" is used in a similar way by many phenomenologists
for that reason, i think the best place to start in seeing how something can be available without being a figure is the apophatic bound

Every thought and perception is finite and limited, but their limitations are only manifest in rare special cases where awareness of the limit amounts to a positive accomplishment (eg, hearing silence, seeing darkness)

You see that you can't see

But blue presents no decomposition. Well technically, brightness saturation & hue. But a small-n number of parts that do not themselves decompose is enough to earn the label "resists" decomposition; this contrasts to the palace or other compound objects, which present countlessly many decompositions

There's no problem with bringing the blue of the blue sky into many-partedness under conjunction. We see it is "the same blue as the banners" or "above the grey-green roof"; or any number of other contextualizations
*That's* the true definition of qualia, I think: Figures which, arising in many-partedness under focal attention, resist the aspect of decomposition

Instead, the modern scruple says, "try to explain"; it conceives of explanation as "accounting for something in terms of the parts"; and then it decomposes the scene under disjunctive many-partedness until it finds parts that don't themselves decompose

What I think happens is that people aren't comfortable with finding the mystery of consciousness in the light touch of partial attention that first brings the palace into view. Although this is already the whole mystery, it can feel like you haven't "tried to find an explanation" if you stop there
And that detail can be disjunctive — the palace its "the front, the sides and the back" or its "marble blocks, wooden beams and nails" — which is, roughly speaking, decomposition into component parts
That detail can be conjuctive — the palace is "from the famous painting" or it "belongs to the queen" — which is, roughly speaking, context
When we focally attend, the thing we attend shows up for us in many-partedness; it presents for us as enriched by arising detail

Phenomenologists have known for a long time what you can discover yourself if you look closely — when we attend to things, we don't reveal what was already fully there; we undertake a creative act where the details we see actively arise for us, having not been there before
My read of the the situation is that moderns historically invested qualia with mystery based on a mistake about the nature of human attention (and lots of other ones too; this of the main one)
